title: Sweet Wine Headache: Why Moscato and Port Hit Hard
excerpt: Why sweet wines like Moscato, port, and sangria give so many people a headache, what the sugar and sulfites really do, and how to drink sweet wine without paying for it.
metaDescription: Why does sweet wine give you a headache? How Moscato, port, sugar, and sulfites play a part, and simple ways to enjoy sweet wine without the pain.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** sweet wine gives a lot of people a headache, but usually not because of the sugar itself. The sugar hides the taste of alcohol, so sweet wines go down fast and easy. Many dessert and fortified wines (port, sherry, Madeira, some late-harvest wines) are also much stronger than table wine, and cheap sweet wines are often poured in big glasses and drunk like juice. Sweet white wines are also allowed to carry more sulfites than dry wines, which matters for the small group of people who react to them. For most social drinkers, the fix is to check the alcohol percentage, pour smaller, slow down, and drink water alongside.

**The quick rules:** Read the ABV (alcohol by volume) on the label before you pour. A light Moscato d'Asti at around 5 to 6 percent is a very different drink from a port at around 20 percent. Pour dessert and fortified wines in small glasses (about 2 to 3 oz), not regular wine glasses. Eat before and while you drink, alternate each glass with water, and stop once the drink starts tasting like dessert rather than wine, because that's when people stop counting.

> **When to see a doctor.** A mild headache after a few glasses of sweet wine is common and usually fades within a day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US)** if you have a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, or a headache with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, vision loss, or fainting. These are not hangover symptoms. Also see a doctor if you get headaches after even a small amount of alcohol on a regular basis, if your headaches are getting more frequent or more severe, or if you have migraines and alcohol keeps setting them off. If you drink heavily most days and get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than stopping suddenly on your own. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Does Sweet Wine Give Me a Headache?

There isn't one single cause. There are several, and they stack. Here they are roughly in order of how often they're likely to matter for an ordinary social drinker.

### 1. The alcohol is easier to drink, so you drink more of it

Sugar is very good at covering up the burn and bitterness of alcohol. That's the whole reason sweet mixers, liqueurs, and dessert wines feel "smooth." The problem is that your body doesn't care how smooth a drink tastes. It responds to the amount of alcohol you take in and how fast you take it in.

When a wine tastes like fruit juice, people tend to:

- sip faster,
- pour bigger glasses,
- accept top-ups without thinking, and
- lose track of how many glasses they've had.

The headache you get from that is mostly an alcohol headache. Alcohol widens blood vessels, makes you pee out more fluid than you take in, breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, and leaves behind acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product your liver makes while breaking alcohol down. All of these can contribute to a headache, and all of them get worse the more you drink. Our [alcohol headache guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains each of these in more detail.

### 2. Many sweet wines are much stronger than you think

"Sweet wine" covers a huge range of drinks, and their alcohol content varies more than most people realize.

| Type of sweet wine | Typical alcohol (check the label) | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Moscato d'Asti (lightly sparkling, Italian) | Often around 5 to 6% | Lowest in alcohol of the common sweet wines |
| Supermarket "Moscato" and sweet blends | Often around 8 to 11% | Easy to drink by the full glass, or the full bottle |
| Sweet Riesling (Spätlese, Auslese) | Often around 8 to 10% | Lighter in alcohol, but sweetness invites big pours |
| Late-harvest wines, Sauternes, Tokaji, ice wine | Often around 10 to 14% | Rich, usually served in small pours, but not always |
| Port, sweet sherry (cream, PX), Madeira, Marsala | Usually around 17 to 20% | Fortified with grape spirit, close to double table wine |
| Sangria, wine coolers, flavored wine drinks | Varies widely | Often mixed with juice, soda, or extra spirits |

The fortified wines at the bottom of that table are the big surprise for many people. Port, sherry, Madeira, and Marsala are made by adding grape spirit (a kind of brandy) to wine, which pushes the alcohol up to around 17 to 20 percent. The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) counts roughly 3 to 4 oz of fortified wine as one standard drink, compared with 5 oz for regular table wine.

So a regular 6 to 8 oz wine glass of port isn't "one glass of wine." It can be closer to two or even three standard drinks. Two of those after dinner, on top of whatever you already had, is a lot of alcohol in a short time. If you want to work out how much you're actually drinking, our guide to [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine) walks through the math.

### 3. Sweet white wines can carry more sulfites

Sulfites (sulfur dioxide and related compounds) are added to almost all wine to keep it from spoiling. In sweet wines, they do an extra job: they help stop leftover sugar from starting to ferment again in the bottle. Because of that, wine rules in the European Union allow higher sulfite limits for sweeter wines than for dry ones, and some classic dessert wines are permitted the highest levels of all. In the US, any wine with more than 10 parts per million of sulfites has to say "contains sulfites" on the label, and the legal maximum is 350 parts per million for all wines.

Here's the honest part. For most people, sulfites are probably not the reason wine gives them a headache. True sulfite sensitivity is uncommon, it mostly affects people with asthma, and the typical reaction is breathing trouble (wheezing, chest tightness), hives, or flushing rather than a classic headache. Many everyday foods, especially dried fruit, contain far more sulfites per serving than a glass of wine. If dried apricots don't bother you, sulfites in wine probably aren't your problem.

That said, if you have asthma and you notice that sweet white wines in particular make you wheezy or flushed, take that seriously and mention it to your doctor. Our [sulfites and wine headaches guide](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) goes through the evidence in full.

### 4. Sugar, alcohol, and your blood sugar

Alcohol changes how your body handles blood sugar. While your liver is busy breaking down alcohol, it's less able to release stored glucose into your blood. For most healthy people this doesn't cause a problem, but after a long night of drinking, especially on an empty stomach, blood sugar can dip lower than normal. Low blood sugar can make you feel shaky, weak, irritable, and headachy.

You might expect that the sugar in sweet wine would protect against that. In practice, it's not that simple. A burst of sugar from a sweet drink can raise blood sugar quickly and then let it fall again, and it doesn't replace a real meal. Researchers have also found that low blood sugar isn't the main driver of most hangovers. So treat this as one possible contributor for some people, not the explanation.

There's one interesting wrinkle worth knowing. A small 2013 study published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* found that people who drank alcohol mixed with diet soda had higher breath alcohol levels than when the same amount was mixed with regular, sugar-sweetened soda. Sugar in the stomach seems to slow down how quickly alcohol reaches the blood. That suggests the sugar in sweet wine isn't adding alcohol to your system. The bigger issue really is that sweet drinks make it easy to drink more.

If you have diabetes, the blood sugar side of drinking is a real safety issue, not just a headache question. Sweet wines can raise your blood sugar at first, and alcohol can then push it dangerously low hours later, sometimes overnight. Talk to your doctor about how alcohol fits with your medication, and see our [alcohol and diabetes guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

### 5. Congeners in fortified and darker sweet wines

Congeners are the extra compounds produced during fermentation and aging that give drinks their flavor and color. Darker drinks generally carry more of them. A well-known 2010 study by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues found that people who drank bourbon reported worse hangovers than people who drank the same amount of vodka, which has very few congeners.

Fortified sweet wines like tawny port, cream sherry, and Madeira are aged, dark, and partly made from spirit, so it's reasonable to think congeners could add to the morning-after headache. But there's no good research that tests sweet wines specifically, so this is a plausible extra, not a proven cause. The amount of alcohol still matters far more.

### 6. Histamine and migraine triggers

Wine contains small amounts of histamine and other compounds called biogenic amines. Most people break these down without noticing. People with a tendency toward histamine intolerance may get flushing, a stuffy nose, or a headache from wine. Levels vary a lot from bottle to bottle, and red wines are usually blamed more than whites, but sweet wines aren't automatically free of them.

Alcohol, and wine in particular, is also one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers. If you have migraines, a sweet wine may simply be a trigger like any other alcoholic drink. Our guides to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) and [migraine after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) cover both in depth.

## Moscato Headache: Why This One Gets So Much Blame

Moscato is probably the sweet wine most people mean when they search for this. It's sweet, fruity, cheap, widely available, and often served very cold. Every one of those things makes it easy to drink quickly.

There are really two different drinks sold as Moscato:

- **Moscato d'Asti** from northern Italy is lightly sparkling and low in alcohol, often around 5 to 6 percent. A glass of it has a lot less alcohol than a glass of Chardonnay. Of all the sweet wines, it's one of the easiest on your head, as long as you don't treat the low alcohol as permission to drink the whole bottle.
- **Supermarket Moscato and "sweet white" blends** are often higher, commonly around 8 to 11 percent. Some are made in big volumes and sold in large bottles or boxes. People often pour these in full glasses and drink them like lemonade.

So when people say "Moscato gives me a headache," the cause is often a mix of: drinking a lot of it quickly because it tastes like juice, drinking it on an empty stomach at a party or brunch, and not drinking much water alongside. If the Moscato is sparkling, the bubbles may also make alcohol reach your blood a little faster. Our [prosecco headache guide](/never-hungover/prosecco-hangover) explains that effect for sparkling wines.

**If you love Moscato and want to keep drinking it:**

1. Choose a true Moscato d'Asti if you can find one, and check that the label says around 5 to 6 percent.
2. Pour a normal-sized glass (5 oz), not a tumbler, and finish it before topping up.
3. Drink a full glass of water between each glass of wine.
4. Eat something with it. Cheese, nuts, or a real meal slow down how fast alcohol is absorbed.

## Dessert Wine and Port Headache

Dessert wines and port tend to show up at the end of a long meal, which is exactly when you've already had wine, maybe a cocktail, and you're tired. That timing is part of the problem. The sweet wine itself may not be the cause. It's the last drink on top of everything else, and often a strong one.

A few things are worth knowing:

- **Port, sherry, and Madeira are fortified.** At around 17 to 20 percent alcohol, a generous pour packs a lot of alcohol. Ask for a small pour, or use a proper small dessert-wine glass.
- **Rich dessert wines like Sauternes and Tokaji** are usually meant to be sipped in small amounts with or after dessert. They're often less alcoholic than port but still stronger than many people assume.
- **Late nights matter.** Drinking late cuts into your sleep, and poor sleep makes almost any hangover headache worse.

A practical rule: if dessert wine is coming at the end of the night, have one small glass, sip it slowly, and drink a large glass of water with it.

## Cheap Sweet Wine, Sangria, and Wine Coolers

Some of the worst "sweet wine headaches" come from drinks that aren't just wine. Sangria, punch, mulled wine, and many party drinks are made by mixing wine with juice, soda, sugar, and sometimes brandy or another spirit. Flavored wine products and wine coolers vary a lot in strength.

These drinks are risky for headaches for a simple reason: you have no idea how much alcohol is in each glass. A pitcher of sangria might be mild, or it might be heavily spiked with brandy. Because it tastes like fruit punch, it's very easy to drink several large glasses without noticing.

If you're at a party with a punch bowl, a good approach is to have one glass, then switch to something where you know the strength, such as a standard glass of wine, a light beer, or a non-alcoholic drink.

## Headache While Drinking vs. the Next Morning

It helps to notice when the headache starts, because the causes are a little different.

**A headache during or soon after drinking (within an hour or two)** points more toward a sensitivity: migraine tendency, histamine reactions, sulfite sensitivity in people with asthma, or the way your body handles acetaldehyde. If even one small glass of sweet wine does this to you regularly, our guide to [getting a headache after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) is a better fit, and it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

**A headache the next morning** is usually a classic hangover. The main drivers are how much alcohol you had, how fast, how well you slept, and whether you ate and drank water. Sweet wine is often a big part of the story only because it made it easy to drink more. For quick relief, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## How to Drink Sweet Wine Without a Headache

None of these tips can promise a headache-free night, because alcohol itself is the main cause of most wine headaches. But they make a real difference for most people.

### Before you drink

- **Eat a proper meal.** Food in your stomach slows down how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Protein, fat, and fiber help most.
- **Start hydrated.** Drink a glass or two of water in the hour before you start.
- **Decide on a limit.** Sweet wine is the easiest kind to over-drink, so it helps to set a number in advance.

### While you drink

- **Read the ABV.** If it's above about 15 percent, treat it like a strong drink and pour accordingly.
- **Use smaller glasses.** About 5 oz for table-strength sweet wines, and about 2 to 3 oz for port, sherry, and other fortified wines.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for every glass of wine is a simple, effective habit.
- **Don't drink it ice cold and fast.** Very cold sweet wine tastes even more like juice. Slow sips help you notice how much you're having.
- **Skip the top-ups.** Finish your glass before anyone refills it, so you can keep count.

### After you drink

- **Drink water before bed.** A large glass helps with the fluid alcohol makes you lose.
- **Eat something in the morning.** Even if you don't feel like it, a simple breakfast helps steady your blood sugar.
- **Use a pain reliever carefully if needed.** An ordinary dose of ibuprofen with food can help a hangover headache for many people, but it can irritate a stomach that's already upset from alcohol. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) carries its own liver warnings around alcohol. Read our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before reaching for it, and don't take any painkiller "just in case" before bed.

## Sweet Wines Least Likely to Give You a Headache

If you like sweet wine and want to keep enjoying it, these choices tend to be gentler:

- **Moscato d'Asti** at around 5 to 6 percent alcohol.
- **German Riesling Kabinett or Spätlese**, which often sit around 8 to 10 percent and are made to balance sweetness with acidity.
- **Small pours of a quality dessert wine** with food, rather than large glasses of cheap sweet wine on their own.

And these are the ones to be more careful with:

- **Port, cream sherry, Madeira, and Marsala** in large pours.
- **Sangria, punches, and mixed wine drinks** of unknown strength.
- **Large-format cheap sweet wines** that are easy to drink by the tumbler.

For a fuller shopping list across all wine styles, see our guide to [wines that don't give you a headache](/never-hungover/wines-that-dont-give-you-a-headache). If dry whites or reds are the ones that bother you, our [white wine headache](/never-hungover/white-wine-headache) and [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) guides go into the specific causes for each.

## What About Supplements Like DHM?

Some people take supplements to support their body during a night of drinking. One of the most popular is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*). Research on DHM is promising but still early. Most of it comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents wine headaches specifically.

If you want to try it, take it as an extra on top of the basics in this guide, not a replacement for them. It won't cancel out a large pour of port. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when. If you take any prescription medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Sweet wine headaches are usually alcohol headaches. The sugar makes the wine easy to drink fast and in large amounts.
- Many sweet wines, especially port, sherry, Madeira, and Marsala, are much stronger than table wine. Check the ABV and pour smaller.
- Sweet white wines can carry more sulfites, but sulfites are a real problem for only a small group of people, mostly those with asthma.
- Moscato d'Asti is one of the lowest-alcohol wines you can buy. Supermarket Moscato and sangria are often stronger and easier to over-drink.
- Eat first, alternate with water, use small glasses, and set a limit before you start.
- See a doctor if headaches come from even small amounts of alcohol, are getting worse, or come with any of the warning signs listed at the top of this page.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does sweet wine give me a headache?**

Usually because the sugar hides the taste of alcohol, so you drink more and faster than you would with a dry wine. Many sweet wines, especially fortified ones like port and sherry, are also stronger than table wine. Sulfites, histamine, congeners, and migraine tendencies can add to it for some people, but the amount of alcohol is the most common cause.

**Does Moscato give you a headache?**

It can, but not because Moscato is uniquely bad. Moscato is sweet, fruity, and often served cold, so it's very easy to drink quickly. Italian Moscato d'Asti is actually low in alcohol (often around 5 to 6 percent), while many supermarket Moscatos are stronger. Pour normal-sized glasses, alternate with water, and eat with it.

**Is it the sugar in wine that causes headaches?**

There is no good evidence that the sugar itself is the main cause of wine headaches. Some research suggests sugar in a drink may even slow down how quickly alcohol reaches the blood. The bigger problem is that sweetness makes it easy to drink more alcohol than you intended. For people with diabetes, though, the blood sugar effects of sweet wine and alcohol are a real safety concern to discuss with a doctor.

**Do sweet wines have more sulfites?**

Often, yes. Sulfites help keep leftover sugar from fermenting again, so sweet white and dessert wines tend to be allowed higher levels, especially under European rules. But true sulfite sensitivity is uncommon and mostly affects people with asthma, who usually notice wheezing or flushing rather than a headache. For most people, sulfites aren't the reason wine causes a headache.

**Why does port or dessert wine give me such a bad headache?**

Port, sherry, Madeira, and Marsala are fortified with grape spirit, which brings them to around 17 to 20 percent alcohol, close to double regular wine. A normal wine glass of port can be two or more standard drinks. Dessert wines also usually come at the end of a long night of drinking, which adds to the total. Ask for small pours of around 2 to 3 oz.

**What's the best sweet wine if I get headaches?**

Lower-alcohol options such as Moscato d'Asti (around 5 to 6 percent) or a German Riesling Kabinett are usually gentler choices. Whatever you pick, the biggest difference comes from how much you drink, how fast, and whether you eat and drink water alongside it.

**How do I get rid of a sweet wine headache?**

Drink water, eat something, and rest. An ordinary dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever with food can help for many people, but read the label warnings about alcohol first. If the headache is sudden and severe, comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness, or vision changes, or doesn't improve within a day, get medical help.

**Can a sweet wine headache be a migraine?**

Yes. Alcohol, including wine, is one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers. If your headache is one-sided, throbbing, and comes with nausea or sensitivity to light and sound, it may be a migraine. If this happens regularly after small amounts of alcohol, talk to a doctor about your triggers and treatment options.
